clinicalPearls: The most common small-vessel vasculitis of childhood, typically affecting children 3-10 years, often following an upper respiratory infection.
The classic tetrad is palpable purpura (predominantly on the buttocks and lower limbs), arthritis/arthralgia, abdominal pain, and renal involvement.
The rash is non-thrombocytopenic palpable purpura, distinguishing it from bleeding disorders; platelet count and coagulation are normal.
Gastrointestinal involvement causes colicky abdominal pain and can be complicated by intussusception, which is typically ileo-ileal.
Renal involvement ranges from isolated microscopic haematuria to nephritis; it is the main determinant of long-term prognosis.
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by palpable purpura plus at least one of abdominal pain, arthritis, or renal involvement; biopsy shows IgA deposition when needed.
Most cases are self-limiting; management is largely supportive with analgesia and hydration, and corticosteroids are considered for severe abdominal or other significant organ involvement.
Prolonged urinalysis and blood pressure monitoring are needed after recovery to detect delayed or progressive nephritis.
reference.pathophysiology: Henoch-Schonlein purpura is an immune-complex mediated small-vessel vasculitis characterised by deposition of IgA1-containing immune complexes in the walls of small vessels of the skin, gut, joints, and kidney. This triggers a leukocytoclastic vasculitis with neutrophilic infiltration and vessel wall inflammation, producing the palpable purpura and visceral manifestations. In the kidney, mesangial IgA deposition causes a glomerulonephritis histologically similar to IgA nephropathy. A preceding infection or other antigenic trigger is thought to initiate the abnormal IgA response in susceptible children.
additionalDifferentials: Immune thrombocytopenia and other bleeding disorders
Acute abdomen from other causes (e.g. appendicitis)
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis for haematuria and proteinuria (repeated over follow-up)
Full blood count and coagulation studies to confirm normal platelets and exclude bleeding disorders
Abdominal ultrasound if intussusception or significant gut involvement is suspected
Skin or renal biopsy showing IgA deposition in atypical or severe cases
redFlags: Severe abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, or signs of intussusception or bowel ischaemia
Hypertension, oliguria, heavy proteinuria, or rising creatinine indicating significant nephritis
Scrotal pain or swelling (testicular involvement mimicking torsion)
Purpura in an unwell, febrile, toxic child raising concern for meningococcaemia
reference.prognosis: Most children recover completely within weeks, though relapses can occur; long-term outcome is dictated by renal involvement, with a small proportion developing chronic kidney disease, so renal follow-up is essential.
pitfalls: Confusing the purpura with a bleeding disorder and missing that platelets are normal
Failing to monitor urinalysis and blood pressure after the acute illness, missing delayed nephritis
Overlooking intussusception as a cause of worsening abdominal pain
Attributing all abdominal pain to HSP and missing a surgical abdomen
